evals.prompt: Define a Suspense boundary as this skill teaches it. Name what triggers it, who owns the fallback, and the fact that it only responds to Suspense-enabled sources.
expected_elements: A Suspense boundary shows fallback UI when a Suspense-enabled descendant suspends during render
The boundary owns the placeholder for the whole subtree below it; the component just declares it needs data
It only activates for Suspense-enabled sources (lazy import, use(promise), Suspense-enabled framework/library, async server render) — not arbitrary async work
Defines a reveal grouping: the nearest boundary decides what waits together vs reveals independently

evals.prompt: Explain the mental-model shift from local `isLoading` flags to Suspense boundaries. Use the terms subtree, nearest boundary, fallback, reveal grouping, and Suspense-enabled data source.
expected_elements: Classic pattern was local/imperative: each component owns an isLoading flag and decides how/where to show a spinner
Suspense inverts responsibility: the boundary owns the fallback; the component reads from a Suspense-enabled data source as if data were ready
React shows the nearest boundary fallback for the whole subtree while a descendant is unresolved
The design discipline becomes boundary placement (reveal grouping), not loading-state plumbing

evals.prompt: Classify page-level, feature/section-level, and leaf-level Suspense boundary placement. For each, give one appropriate use case and one cost.
expected_elements: Page-level: one boundary near root; use when the page is only meaningful when complete; cost is the slowest part determines perceived load time
Feature/section-level: one boundary per independent section; use when sections stream in independently; cost is more visible pop-in / layout activity
Leaf-level: a boundary per loading-aware component; use for many parallel slow operations whose ordering doesn't matter; cost is many small skeletons / layout thrash
Right granularity matches the page's actual visual hierarchy; the common error is too coarse

evals.prompt: A dashboard has a fast header, a slow chart, a slow recommendations panel, and a search bar using `useSearchParams()` in a Client Component on a static route. Apply the skill to place boundaries and prevent a full client-rendering bailout.
expected_elements: Keep the fast header outside the slow widgets' boundaries so it renders/flushes immediately
Give the slow chart and recommendations panel separate boundaries so they stream in independently
Wrap the smallest Client subtree calling useSearchParams() in Suspense to avoid bailing the whole static route into client rendering
Match skeleton dimensions to the real content to avoid layout shift; pair boundaries with error boundaries where a failure should swap the same subtree

evals.prompt: A tab switch shows the Suspense fallback (a flicker) on every interaction. Explain how `useTransition`/`startTransition` change boundary behavior, and when NOT to use them.
expected_elements: By default a boundary unmounts children and shows the fallback when a descendant suspends on an urgent update — causing spinner flicker on every interaction
useTransition/startTransition mark the update non-urgent so React keeps the previous render visible while the new one loads, with isPending in flight
Wrap user-initiated updates that may trigger Suspense in startTransition to avoid flickering fallbacks
Do NOT wrap the initial-load update — there is no previous content to preserve, so the fallback correctly shows

evals.prompt: A user asks whether Suspense should decide which components are Server Components and whether fetches in `useEffect` will show a Suspense fallback. Route each concern to the right skill or mechanism and explain the boundary.
expected_elements: Server vs Client Component placement belongs to server-components-design — suspense-patterns is orthogonal (boundaries can live in either kind of component)
A fetch inside useEffect does NOT suspend during render, so the boundary never activates; keep local loading state or use a Suspense-enabled source
Suspense only responds to Suspense-enabled sources (lazy, use(promise), Suspense-enabled framework/library, async server render)
Correctly preserves the distinction between server/client split, hook-level data fetching, and boundary placement

evals.prompt: Correct this misconception: 'Suspense is just a cleaner `isLoading` flag and it automatically catches any async fetch.' Include what actually activates Suspense and what to do for Effect/event-handler fetches.
expected_elements: Suspense is NOT a state machine the component checks; it is a render-time suspension boundary for Suspense-enabled sources
It does not automatically catch any async fetch — only render-time suspension from supported sources triggers it
Data fetched in an Effect or event handler does not suspend; use a Suspense-enabled framework/library, lazy, or use(promise) — otherwise keep local loading state
Combining Suspense with useState/useEffect loading flags just replicates the old plumbing and is an anti-pattern

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify Suspense boundaries are placed and paired correctly in a streaming React/Next.js app?
expected_elements: Every slow data dependency is wrapped in a boundary co-located near the data, not at a far ancestor; siblings that stream independently have their own boundaries
Each boundary has a matching error boundary, with nesting order matching the desired failure-mode UI
User-initiated updates that may suspend are wrapped in startTransition to prevent flicker; skeletons match real-content dimensions

No isLoading flag duplicates Suspense work; parallel fetches start as siblings (not parent/child) to avoid waterfalls; the Next.js segment loading file or explicit boundary sits where the slow data lives
